entry.title: The Falling Cost of Intelligence: How AI Is Becoming Exponentially Cheaper and What It Means for Enterprises
entry.content:
A model that performed at GPT-3.5 level cost about $20 per million tokens in November 2022. By October 2024, the same level of performance cost about $0.07. That is a drop of more than 280 times in under two years, according to the Stanford AI Index 2025.

Source: Generated using AI

Yet many enterprise AI bills are growing, not shrinking. Both things are true at once, and understanding why is the difference between a sensible AI cost strategy and a surprising invoice.

This article looks at how fast the cost of AI inference is falling, what is driving it, where the numbers can mislead you, and what engineering and finance teams should do about it. The title says “exponentially”. That word is fair for the price of a fixed level of capability, which falls in a roughly straight line on a log chart. It is not fair for every model or every price list, and the difference matters.

Three different things people call the cost of AI

Most confusion about AI pricing comes from mixing up three separate measurements.

  • Cost per token: what you pay to process or generate one token. This is the number on the pricing page.
  • Cost per task: what you pay to finish a piece of work, such as summarizing a contract or resolving a card dispute. It depends on how many tokens the task consumes and how often it has to be retried.
  • Cost per unit of intelligence: what you pay to reach a given quality bar, for example a score on a benchmark. This is the number that tells you whether AI itself is getting cheaper.

The first has fallen sharply at every tier. The third has fallen even more dramatically. The second depends on your workload, and it is the one your CFO actually sees.

What the price lists show

OpenAI’s history gives a clean timeline because the company has published list prices for every generation. The table uses standard rates in USD per million tokens, taken from OpenAI’s pricing page and launch-time list prices.

Model Input per 1M tokens Output per 1M tokens Released
GPT-4 $30.00 $60.00 March 2023
GPT-4o $5.00 $15.00 May 2024
GPT-4.1 $2.00 $8.00 April 2025 (announcement)
GPT-6 Astra $10.00 $50.00 September 2026
GPT-6.1 Sol $2.00 $10.00 September 2026
GPT-6 Luna $0.10 $0.50 September 2026

Astra reached the API on September 3, 2026. Sol and Luna followed in late September at half the price of their GPT-5.6 predecessors, with OpenAI attributing the cut to improvements in caching and inference.

The arithmetic is striking. GPT-4 to GPT-4o made input 6 times cheaper and output 4 times cheaper. GPT-4o to GPT-4.1 added another 2.5 times on input and about 1.9 times on output. GPT-4 to GPT-6 Luna is 300 times cheaper on input and 120 times cheaper on output at standard rates.

Two warnings apply before anyone puts those numbers on a slide.

First, these are different capability tiers, not the same model getting cheaper. GPT-6 Luna is not GPT-4 at a discount.

Second, look at the top of the table. Astra’s input price is 3 times lower than GPT-4’s launch price, but its output price is only about 1.2 times lower. The frontier price has barely moved. What collapsed is the price of yesterday’s capability. The newest and strongest model still costs real money, and it is priced in the same range as the top tiers from other labs. Anthropic’s top tier sat at $10 and $50 for Claude Fable 5.1, then dropped to $8 and $40 for Fable 5.2.

[Suggested visual: log-scale chart of OpenAI list prices by model release date, with the frontier tier and the small tier plotted as separate lines]

The same pattern appears across vendors

Anthropic’s published pricing shows the same shape when you compare tiers across generations.

Tier Earlier generation (input / output per 1M) Current generation (input / output per 1M) Caveat
Large Claude Opus 4.1: $15 / $75 Claude Opus 5.5: $4 / $20 Different capability levels
Mid Claude Sonnet 4.6: $3 / $15 Claude Sonnet 5.5: $2 / $10 Newer tokenizer produces about 30% more tokens for the same text
Small Claude Haiku 4.5: $1 / $5 Claude Haiku 5.5: $0.10 / $0.50 Prompts over 100,000 tokens are priced at $0.50 / $2.50

The figures come from Anthropic’s pricing documentation. Google showed the earlier version of this behavior when it cut Gemini 1.5 Pro prices by 64% on input and 52% on output for prompts under 128K tokens in October 2024.

The tokenizer note in the table is easy to miss and worth remembering. Anthropic states that Claude 4.7 and later models produce roughly 30% more tokens for the same text than earlier ones. A lower price per token does not automatically mean a lower price per document. Comparing vendors on price per million tokens is only a first approximation.

Intelligence is getting cheaper, not just tokens

A price list compares different models. A better question is how much it costs to buy a fixed level of capability over time. Several independent efforts have tried to measure that.

The Stanford AI Index 2025, using data from Epoch AI and Artificial Analysis, found that the cost of querying a model at roughly GPT-3.5 level on the MMLU benchmark fell from $20 to $0.07 per million tokens between November 2022 and October 2024. Stanford attributes the drop to increasingly capable small models. On a harder benchmark, GPQA, the cost of reaching above 50% fell from $15 per million tokens in May 2024 to $0.12 in December 2024, which is about 125 times in seven months.

Epoch AI’s analysis of inference price trends puts the rate of decline between 9 times and 900 times per year, depending on the performance threshold. For example, the price of matching GPT-4’s score on PhD-level science questions fell by about 40 times per year.

There are good reasons to hold these numbers loosely:

  • The extreme end of the range rests on few data points. Epoch itself notes that the fastest declines happened recently and it is less clear they will persist.
  • Benchmarks saturate. Once many models pass a test, the price of “passing” stops telling you much about harder work.
  • Price per token is not cost per solved problem. An MIT FutureTech study, The Price of Progress, points out that reasoning models can have a lower per-token cost but a larger overall cost because they generate more tokens. It also cites separate work finding that the cost to solve benchmark problems fell much more slowly on harder tests, by about 24.5 times per year on MATH-500 but only about 3.2 times per year on AIME 2024.

So the honest summary is this. At a fixed, well-defined capability level, cost is falling very fast. For the hardest tasks, where the frontier is the only option, it is falling much more slowly.

Why the cost keeps falling

No single breakthrough explains the trend. Several independent improvements stack, and competition pushes providers to pass some of the savings on.

flowchart LR subgraph SUPPLY[“Cost to produce a token”] H[“Hardware generations”] M[“Sparse architectures such as MoE”] Q[“Quantization”] S[“Batching and prompt caching”] end subgraph CAPABILITY[“Cost to reach a quality bar”] D[“Distillation into smaller models”] T[“Better training recipes and data”] end C[“Competition and open-weight models”] P([“Lower price at fixed capability”]) E{“Does usage grow faster than price falls?”} U[“Total AI spend rises”] F[“Total AI spend falls”] H –> P M –> P Q –> P S –> P D –> P T –> P C –> P P –> E E –>|Yes| U E –>|No| F classDef execution fill:#E5F6F1,stroke:#65B9A1,color:#205B4C,stroke-width:2px classDef processing fill:#EEE9FF,stroke:#9985D5,color:#493878,stroke-width:2px classDef primary fill:#EAF2FF,stroke:#6495D0,color:#243B60,stroke-width:2px classDef decision fill:#FFF5DC,stroke:#D9A441,color:#74500B,stroke-width:2px classDef results fill:#FCECF4,stroke:#D88BB0,color:#743C58,stroke-width:2px classDef success fill:#E5F5E9,stroke:#75B887,color:#285B35,stroke-width:2px class H,Q,S execution class M,D,T processing class C primary class P success class E decision class U,F results style SUPPLY fill:#FFFFFF,stroke:#79ACD6,stroke-width:2px style CAPABILITY fill:#FFFFFF,stroke:#79ACD6,stroke-width:2px
Driver What it changes Evidence Catch
Hardware generations More tokens per second per dollar and per watt Stanford’s AI Index 2025 summarizes ML hardware costs falling about 30% per year and energy efficiency improving about 40% per year Savings reach customers only if competition forces providers to pass them on
Sparse architectures (MoE) Fewer active parameters per token Widely used technique, though closed-model details are rarely published All experts still need memory, so the serving footprint stays large
Quantization Smaller weights and cache, higher throughput Standard serving optimization Quality can degrade on edge cases, so it needs evaluation
Caching and batching Reuses prefix work and keeps GPUs busy OpenAI lists cached input for Astra at $1 versus $10 standard; Flex and Batch rates are half of standard Needs stable prompt prefixes; batch work waits longer
Distillation Small models imitate larger ones Stanford links the GPT-3.5-level cost drop to capable small models Students rarely match teachers on the hard tail of tasks
Competition Pricing pressure across labs and open-weight models The Gemini 1.5 Pro cut in 2024 and the 50% GPT-6 Sol and Luna cuts in 2026 Providers can also keep efficiency gains as margin

Compute per token and bytes per token

During generation, a large model spends much of its time moving weights and cached attention data through memory rather than doing arithmetic. That is why several of these techniques work.

A mixture-of-experts model routes each token through a small subset of its parameters. Compute per token falls, though the whole model still has to sit in memory. Quantization stores weights, and sometimes the attention cache, in fewer bits. Less data to move means more tokens per second on the same chip. The price is a small but real risk of quality loss that only shows up when you test against your own tasks.

Batching and prompt caching

A GPU is cheapest to run when it is busy. Providers group many requests together so the hardware stays utilized. The tradeoff is latency, which is why speed is now a priced feature. OpenAI lists a Fast mode for Astra at $20 and $100, double the standard rate. Anthropic prices fast mode for Claude Opus 5.5 at twice standard as well.

Prompt caching works because transformer models compute intermediate attention state for every token they read. If the next request starts with the same long prefix, a provider can reuse that state instead of recomputing it. This describes the general mechanism, not any one vendor’s implementation. The price effect is public: cached input for Astra is $1 per million tokens versus $10, and on Claude Sonnet 5.5 a cache read costs 5% of the base input price.

What this looks like in real money

Take a hypothetical application that processes 1 million input tokens and 250,000 output tokens. Input-heavy workloads are typical. Snowflake’s AI research team has observed roughly 10 to 1 ratios between prompt and generated tokens across many enterprise workloads.

Model Input (1M tokens) Output (250K tokens) Total
GPT-4 $30.00 $15.00 $45.00
GPT-4o $5.00 $3.75 $8.75
GPT-4.1 $2.00 $2.00 $4.00
GPT-6 Astra $10.00 $12.50 $22.50
GPT-6.1 Sol $2.00 $2.50 $4.50
GPT-6 Luna $0.10 $0.125 $0.225

Choosing the right tier matters as much as choosing the newest model. Astra costs 100 times more than Luna for the same token volume, and the model released today at the top of the range is not cheaper than GPT-4.1 from 2025.

Now scale it up. Consider a bank that uses an LLM to process debit-card disputes. Assume 10 million claims a year, with 5,000 input tokens and 1,000 output tokens per claim. That is 50 billion input tokens and 10 billion output tokens annually. These are illustrative assumptions, not a forecast.

Model Cost per claim Annual cost Reading
GPT-4 $0.21 $2,100,000 Pricing from 2023
GPT-4o $0.04 $400,000 Roughly 5 times cheaper than GPT-4
GPT-4.1 $0.018 $180,000 Roughly 12 times cheaper than GPT-4
GPT-6 Astra $0.10 $1,000,000 Frontier capability at frontier price
GPT-6.1 Sol $0.02 $200,000 Mid-tier for demanding coding and agent work
GPT-6 Luna $0.001 $10,000 High-volume tier for focused tasks

Standard rates are assumed throughout. Flex and Batch processing roughly halve every figure for work that can wait, so Astra drops to about $500,000 and Luna to about $5,000.

Caching changes the picture further. Suppose 80% of each prompt is a stable policy manual and examples that hit the cache on Sol. Input cost falls from $100,000 to about $24,000 (10 billion uncached tokens at $2, plus 40 billion cached tokens at $0.10 per million). The total becomes about $124,000. Output, now $100,000, dominates the bill. Once input is cached, the length of the answer is the main cost lever.

Cheaper tokens do not always mean cheaper outcomes

A $0.001 claim sounds like a bargain until the cheap model gets the answer wrong.

The metric that matters to a business is cost per successful outcome:

cost per successful outcome = total AI operating cost / successfully completed tasks</p>

<p>total AI operating cost = token cost + retries + human review + rework + incident cost

Here is a worked example, with assumptions stated. A small model costs $0.001 per claim and resolves 70% of claims correctly. A frontier model costs $0.10 per claim and resolves 98%. Each failed claim needs a human to fix it, at an assumed $8.

  • Small model: $0.001 + 0.30 × $8 = about $2.40 per claim.
  • Frontier model: $0.10 + 0.02 × $8 = about $0.26 per claim.

The frontier model costs 100 times more in tokens and is about 9 times cheaper per claim. Across 10 million claims that is roughly $24 million versus $2.6 million. The result flips if the cheap model’s accuracy is close to the expensive model’s, or if human review is cheap. The only way to know is to measure accuracy on your own tasks.

Where the arithmetic gets messy

  • Reasoning tokens. Reasoning models produce hidden thinking tokens that are billed as output. A cheap per-token price can still produce an expensive answer, as the MIT study above notes.
  • Agent loops. An agent that makes 20 model calls, each re-sending 30,000 tokens of context, consumes about 600,000 input tokens for one task. At $2 per million that is $1.20 for the task, against a cent or two for a single claim. With 90% cache hits it falls to about $0.18, but it never reaches the cost of a single call.
  • Tokenizers. The same document can be a different number of tokens on different models, as the Claude tokenizer note showed.
  • Long context. Some price lists change above a prompt-length threshold. Claude Haiku 5.5 lists five times the standard rate above 100,000 tokens.

The deeper point is Jevons-style. When a resource gets cheaper, people use more of it. Cheaper tokens encourage more agents, longer contexts and more automated workflows. Unit cost can fall 100 times while total spend rises, which is why many teams see bills grow during a period of falling prices.

Engineering for a falling cost curve

If unit prices keep falling, the right architecture is one that can move work between tiers as prices and quality change. The practical pattern is a model cascade: try a cheaper model first, validate the result, and escalate only when needed.

flowchart TD A([“Incoming task”]) B[“Classifier for complexity and risk”] C{“Complexity and risk level”} D[“Small model”] E[“Mid-tier model”] F[“Frontier model”] G{“Validator passes?”} H{“Validator passes?”} I{“Policy and confidence check”} J[“Human review”] K([“Accepted result”]) L[“Log cost, tokens and outcome”] A –> B B –> C C –>|Low| D C –>|Medium| E C –>|High| F D –> G G –>|Pass| K G –>|Fail| E E –> H H –>|Pass| K H –>|Fail| F F –> I I –>|Pass| K I –>|Fail| J J –> K K –> L classDef primary fill:#EAF2FF,stroke:#6495D0,color:#243B60,stroke-width:2px classDef context fill:#EDF7FF,stroke:#79ACD6,color:#244968,stroke-width:2px classDef processing fill:#EEE9FF,stroke:#9985D5,color:#493878,stroke-width:2px classDef decision fill:#FFF5DC,stroke:#D9A441,color:#74500B,stroke-width:2px classDef review fill:#E7F5FC,stroke:#76B5D2,color:#24546C,stroke-width:2px classDef success fill:#E5F5E9,stroke:#75B887,color:#285B35,stroke-width:2px class A primary class B,L context class D,E,F processing class C,G,H,I decision class J review class K success

The cascade’s expected cost is easy to model. The following Python sketch is illustrative, not production code. It assumes a validator that reliably detects failures and that each tier’s success rate applies to the tasks it actually receives. In practice, tasks that escape a small model are usually harder than average, so measured success rates on escalated cases will be lower.

from dataclasses import dataclass</p>

<p>@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Tier:
    name: str
    input_per_m: float    # USD per 1M input tokens
    output_per_m: float   # USD per 1M output tokens
    success_rate: float   # measured on your own evaluation set</p>

<p>def token_cost(tier: Tier, tokens_in: int, tokens_out: int) -> float:
    return (tokens_in * tier.input_per_m + tokens_out * tier.output_per_m) / 1_000_000</p>

<p>def expected_cost(tiers: list[Tier], tokens_in: int, tokens_out: int, human_cost: float) -> float:
    “”“Expected cost per task when tiers are tried in order and failures escalate.”“”
    cost, p_reach = 0.0, 1.0
    for tier in tiers:
        cost += p_reach * token_cost(tier, tokens_in, tokens_out)
        p_reach *= 1 - tier.success_rate      # share of tasks that fail this tier
    return cost + p_reach * human_cost         # leftover failures go to a human</p>

<p>small = Tier(“small”, 0.10, 0.50, 0.70)
frontier = Tier(“frontier”, 10.00, 50.00, 0.98)</p>

<p>print(expected_cost([small], 5_000, 1_000, 8.0))            # about 2.40
print(expected_cost([frontier], 5_000, 1_000, 8.0))         # about 0.26
print(expected_cost([small, frontier], 5_000, 1_000, 8.0))  # about 0.079

With the earlier assumptions, the cascade costs about $0.08 per claim. That beats both single-model options, but only because the validator is trustworthy. A weak validator turns a cost optimization into a quality problem.

Caching deserves the same care. The stable part of the prompt must be identical from one request to the next, so the variable part goes last. This pseudocode shows the idea.

</p>

<a name="Pseudocode:.keep.the.shared.prefix.byte-identical.so.it.can.be.cached"></a>
<h1>Pseudocode: keep the shared prefix byte-identical so it can be cached</h1>

<p>def build_prompt(claim):
    return [
        {“role”: “system”, “content”: POLICY_MANUAL + FEW_SHOT_EXAMPLES},  # same on every call
        {“role”: “user”, “content”: render(claim)},                         # changes on every call
    ]

Providers differ in how they enable this. Anthropic documents a cache_control field, and OpenAI’s docs have a guide on keeping the prompt prefix unchanged. Check each vendor’s current documentation for the exact behavior.

Which tactics fit which situation

Tactic What it saves What it risks Best fit
Smaller tier for routine work Up to two orders of magnitude on token cost Lower accuracy on ambiguous cases Classification, extraction, routing
Cascade with validators Frontier spend on only the hard cases Weak validators, added latency and complexity Mixed-difficulty, high-volume queues
Prompt caching Up to 90% on repeated input Savings vanish if prefixes change Long shared instructions or documents
Batch or Flex processing About 50% on list price Results arrive later Overnight reports, backfills, evaluations
Shorter prompts and retrieval Input tokens and latency Missed context if retrieval is poor Large knowledge bases
Self-hosted open-weight models Per-token fees at high, steady volume Capacity planning, security and operations burden Predictable load and strong platform teams

Token efficiency is becoming an engineering metric in its own right. Useful numbers to track are tokens per task, cache hit rate, escalation rate, retries, and cost per successful outcome. Without them you cannot tell whether a price cut helped.

Risks and limits of the cost curve

Prices are not fixed, and promotions end. OpenAI’s page notes that GPT-5.6 Sol’s promotional pricing runs only until November 30, 2026. Models are deprecated and replaced, and a forced migration is an engineering cost even when the new model is cheaper.

A cheaper model is a different model. Swapping tiers changes output style, failure modes and sometimes refusal behavior. Without a regression suite you will learn about the difference from customers. For regulated work such as banking, a cost-driven model change may need its own review.

Hidden multipliers. Regional processing for newer OpenAI models carries a 10% uplift, and Anthropic applies a 1.1 times multiplier for US-only inference. Speed premiums double the rate. These adjustments can erase part of a headline discount.

Efficiency gains are not guaranteed to reach you. The savings from better hardware and serving can be passed on, kept as margin, or spent on larger models. Stanford’s cost-per-capability data shows the net effect so far, but it does not guarantee the future.

Budget governance lags adoption. Because usage tends to grow faster than price falls, teams that budget by token price alone are surprised by total spend.

Where the curve may go next

It helps to separate what is demonstrated from what is hoped for.

  • Demonstrated: Orders-of-magnitude declines in the price of fixed capability since 2022, as measured by Stanford and Epoch AI. Frontier-tier prices that stay roughly flat while older capability collapses.
  • Deployed: Prompt caching, batch discounts, small and mid-tier models for high-volume work, and routing patterns in production systems.
  • Research: Algorithmic efficiency gains, cheaper long-context handling, and better methods for making reasoning use fewer tokens. The Price of Progress study estimates how much of the decline comes from algorithms and how much from hardware and economics.
  • Speculative: That current rates of decline continue for many more years. Epoch’s own caution applies. The fastest drops were recent, and rates tend to slow as a capability level ages.

For the strongest claims to come true, hardware efficiency must keep improving, small models must keep closing the gap on hard tasks, and competition must stay intense enough that providers pass savings on. Any of those could weaken.

What enterprises should do differently

The opportunity is bigger than saving money on today’s workloads. As the cost of a capability falls, tasks that were uneconomic to automate become viable. Document review, claims triage and internal search might not have cleared a business case three years ago and might clear it now.

A practical approach is to keep a short list of workflows that failed on cost and re-run the numbers every quarter. Build routing and evaluation first, so a cheaper model can be adopted in days rather than months. Negotiate contracts around capability and outcomes instead of fixed per-token rates that will look expensive within a year.

Key takeaways

  • Token prices are falling, and the price of a fixed level of capability is falling much faster. Stanford documents a drop of more than 280 times for GPT-3.5-level performance in under two years, and Epoch AI reports declines of 9 to 900 times per year depending on the threshold.
  • The frontier is not getting cheap at the same rate. The newest top-tier models still cost around $10 and $50 per million tokens.
  • Cost per token, cost per task and cost per unit of intelligence are different measurements. Cost per successful outcome is the one that belongs in a business case.
  • A model cascade with validators, prompt caching and batch processing turn falling prices into real savings. Without measurement they can also hide quality problems.
  • Lower unit cost does not guarantee lower total spend. Cheaper tokens invite more usage, and total consumption can grow faster than prices fall.

The price of intelligence is dropping quickly, but the price of being wrong is not. The teams that benefit most will be the ones that can measure outcomes, switch models safely, and spend the savings on problems that were previously out of reach.

entry.title: The Code That Bit Back: Surviving AI's Jagged Frontier in Code Reviews
entry.content:
I remember the day our shiny new AI code reviewer went live like it was yesterday. It was a Tuesday in early 2025, and our team at EchoSoft—a mid-sized dev shop cranking out enterprise apps—had just pushed the button on integrating GPT-4o into our GitHub Actions pipeline. We’d spent weeks fine-tuning prompts, benchmarking against human reviewers, and celebrating how it slashed review times from hours to minutes. “This is it,” I told the devs over Slack. “No more blocking PRs on nitpicks.” We high-fived virtually, popped a bottle of virtual champagne, and watched the first few PRs sail through with glowing approvals.

Then came PR #478 from junior dev Alex. A simple refactor of our auth module—nothing fancy, just swapping out a deprecated hash function for Argon2. The AI scanned it in seconds: “LGTM! Solid upgrade, no security flags.” Alex merged it. By Friday, our staging server was compromised. Attackers exploited a buffer overflow the AI had glossed over because, in its infinite wisdom, it hallucinated that our input sanitization was “enterprise-grade” based on a snippet from some outdated Stack Overflow thread it pulled from thin air. We lost a weekend scrubbing logs, notifying users, and patching the hole. The client? They bailed, citing “unreliable tooling.” That stung. We’d bet the farm on AI being our force multiplier, but it turned out to be a loaded gun.

Why did this happen? Not because we picked a bad model—GPT-4o was crushing benchmarks left and right. No, it was the jaggedness. That term had been buzzing in AI circles for months, ever since Ethan Mollick’s piece laid it out clear as day: AI doesn’t progress smoothly like a rising tide; it advances in fits and starts, acing PhD-level theorem proving one minute and fumbling basic if-else logic the next. Our code reviewer was a poster child for it—flawless on boilerplate CRUD ops, but a disaster on edge-case vulns that humans spot with a coffee-fueled squint. We’d ignored the warning signs during our proof-of-concept phase, too dazzled by the 95% accuracy on synthetic datasets. In production, though? The cracks showed fast.

The breach wasn’t just embarrassing; it cost us $150K in incident response and lost revenue. But more than that, it forced us to confront how we’d romanticized AI. We’d treated it like a senior engineer, not a quirky intern who occasionally sets the break room on fire. As I pored over the post-mortem with our CTO, Sarah, she leaned back and said, “This isn’t about the model. It’s about expecting consistency where there isn’t any.” She was right. Jagged intelligence isn’t a bug; it’s the architecture. LLMs scale parameters into the trillions, gobbling up patterns from the internet’s firehose, but they don’t “understand” in the human sense. They predict tokens probabilistically, which means they’re probabilistic gamblers at heart—great odds on the favorites, but they’ll bet the house on long shots and lose.

That night, I couldn’t sleep. I fired up my laptop and started digging, not just into our logs, but into the broader mess of AI reliability. What I found was a horror show of uneven performance that made our fiasco feel almost pedestrian.

Digging into the Dirt: What the Data Told Us

Monday morning, I rallied the team for an all-hands autopsy. We pulled every PR from the past three months—about 2,300 in total—and ran them through a custom eval script I’d hacked together overnight. It cross-referenced AI approvals against human audits and static analyzers like SonarQube. The results? A brutal wake-up.

On straightforward changes—think variable renames or adding a new endpoint—our AI nailed it 98% of the time. Faster than any human, too; reviews clocked in at 12 seconds versus 45 minutes for a senior dev. But zoom in on anything remotely tricky, like concurrency bugs or crypto mishandlings, and the accuracy plummeted to 42%. Worse, in 28% of those cases, it didn’t just miss the issue—it fabricated fixes. “Your mutex lock looks good here,” it’d say, when the code was wide open to race conditions. Hallucinations, plain and simple.

I wasn’t shocked, exactly, but the numbers hit hard. We’d benchmarked against public datasets like HumanEval, where GPT-4o scores 85% on coding tasks. But those are toy problems, sanitized for academia. In the wild? A 2025 Vectara leaderboard pegged hallucination rates for top LLMs at 6.3% for Gemini 2.5 Flash on grounded queries, but spiking to 16% for Claude 3.7 Sonnet—and that’s in controlled settings. Our production logs showed worse: 35% overall, ballooning to 65% on security-sensitive PRs. Why the delta? Jaggedness rears its head in domain specificity. Models trained on vast corpora excel at general syntax but choke on niche patterns like zero-day vuln signatures, where the training data thins out.

We sliced the data further. Using pandas in a Jupyter notebook, I grouped failures by code complexity (measured via cyclomatic score) and query type. Here’s a snippet of what that looked like:

import pandas as pd
from radon.complexity import cc_visit

df = pd.read_csv('pr_logs.csv')
df['complexity'] = df['code_snippet'].apply(lambda x: cc_visit(x)[0] if x else 0)
df['hallucinated'] = df['ai_response'].str.contains('fabricated', na=False)

high_complex = df[df['complexity'] > 10]
print(high_complex['hallucinated'].mean())  # Output: 0.65

That 65%? It correlated with low-confidence tokens in the model’s output—stuff below 0.7 probability, which we could’ve flagged but didn’t. Broader industry stats backed this up. Stanford’s HAI crew dropped a bomb in mid-2025: LLMs hallucinate 69% to 88% on legal queries, a proxy for precision-heavy domains like code security. And in a Nature study from August, multi-model tests clocked hallucination at 50% to 82% across prompting strategies. Even the shiny new ones aren’t immune; AIMultiple’s 2026 preview (yeah, they jump the gun) shows latest models hovering above 15% on statement analysis.

Then there’s the DevOps angle. The 2025 DORA report— that bible for us pipeline jockeys—hammered home how AI amplifies your org’s chaos. Elite teams using AI-assisted tools saw 2.5x faster deployments, but low performers? They tanked reliability by 40%, thanks to unchecked jagged outputs eroding trust. Our shop was mid-tier at best; we’d leaned on AI to punch above our weight, but without guardrails, it exposed our gaps. Rhetorical question: If even Google’s Gemini flashes a 0.7% hallucination rate in ideal conditions, what hope do we mortals have in the trenches?

The investigation stretched two weeks. We interviewed users (devs griping about “ghost suggestions”), audited training data (too generic, missing our React-Native stack), and even spun up A/B tests routing half our PRs through the AI, half manual. The verdict? Jaggedness isn’t random—it’s predictable if you look for bottlenecks like sparse data or over-reliance on autoregression. By week’s end, we had a heatmap of failure modes: red blobs on async patterns, crypto, and third-party integrations. It wasn’t despair; it was clarity. Time to fix this beast.

Wrangling the Beast: Building a Jagged-Proof Pipeline

Sarah greenlit a war chest for the rebuild: $80K budget, two engineers reassigned, and me leading the charge. No more blind faith in black-box APIs. We needed a hybrid system—AI for the grunt work, humans and rules for the sharp edges. The core pivot? Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG, to ground the model’s wild guesses in our own knowledge base.

First, we stood up a vector store with Pinecone, indexing our entire repo history, past vulns from OWASP, and synthetic edge cases generated via a fine-tuned Llama 3.1. The idea: Before the AI opines on a PR diff, it queries the store for similar snippets, injecting relevant context into the prompt. Trade-off? Latency jumped from 12 seconds to 28, but accuracy? We’d see.

Here’s the meat of it, in Python with LangChain:

from langchain_openai import ChatOpenAI
from langchain_pinecone import PineconeVectorStore
from langchain.chains import RetrievalQA
from langchain.prompts import PromptTemplate

# Load vector store with our indexed code/vulns
vectorstore = PineconeVectorStore.from_existing_index(
    index_name="code-vulns", embedding=OpenAIEmbeddings()
)

# Custom prompt to enforce grounding
prompt = PromptTemplate(
    template="""Based solely on the following context: {context}
Review this code diff: {diff}
Flag any security issues with evidence from context. If unsure, defer to human.""",
    input_variables=["context", "diff"]
)

llm = ChatOpenAI(model="gpt-4o", temperature=0.1)  # Low temp for determinism
qa_chain = RetrievalQA.from_chain_type(
    llm=llm, chain_type="stuff", retriever=vectorstore.as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 5})
)

# In pipeline: response = qa_chain.run(diff=pr_diff)

This wasn’t plug-and-play. Indexing 500K lines of code took a weekend, and tuning the retriever’s k (top-k matches) meant balancing recall versus noise—too many chunks, and the prompt hit token limits; too few, and we missed analogs. We iterated with A/B: Version 1 used cosine similarity; switched to Euclidean after it favored syntactic fluff over semantic risks.

Layer two: Guardrails. Pure RAG trusts the LLM too much, so we bolted on rule-based checks via Semgrep for static patterns (e.g., SQL injection regexes) and a confidence scorer. If the AI’s output had >20% low-prob tokens or contradicted the retrieved context, it’d flag for human review. Architectural hurdle? Integrating this into GitHub Actions without bloating CI times. We offloaded heavy lifts to a sidecar Lambda, async-ing the RAG query. Cost? Peaked at $0.02 per PR, peanuts compared to breach fallout.

Skeptical as ever, I pushed for ablation tests. Strip RAG? Hallucinations back to 35%. Ditch guardrails? False approvals spike 22%. The combo? Preliminary evals showed 78% accuracy on our high-complexity set—better, but not bulletproof. We also fine-tuned a smaller model (Mistral 7B) on 10K labeled PRs, distilling GPT’s knowledge into something lighter. Transfer learning shaved 15% off inference costs, per our AWS bills.

Rollout was cautious: Canary to 20% of PRs, monitor for a sprint. Bugs? Plenty—like the retriever pulling irrelevant Node.js snippets for our Python monorepo. Fixed with metadata filtering: filter={"language": "python"}. By month two, it was humming.

The Smoke Clears: Metrics, Mayhem, and One Big Takeaway

Three months post-rebuild, and the pipeline’s a different animal. PR throughput? Up 40%, from 15 to 21 merges per dev per week. Human review tickets? Down 62%, freeing seniors for architecture instead of bike-shedding. On security, the win was stark: Zero hallucinated approvals in 1,200 PRs, versus four breaches (minor, thank god) in the prior quarter. Our custom benchmark—mirroring that Nature study’s hallucination gauntlet—clocked the hybrid at 12% error rate, a 70% drop from vanilla GPT. Client satisfaction? Back to 92%, per NPS surveys, and we clawed back that lost account with a demo of the “fortified” reviewer.

The DORA metrics tell a fuller story. Pre-jagged fix, we were laggards: 45-day lead times, 12% change failure rate. Post? Elite territory—18 days, 4% failures—thanks to AI amplifying our disciplined bits, not the sloppy ones. But here’s the rub: It took engineering sweat to get here. RAG maintenance? Ongoing, as code evolves. Guardrails evolve too, or they ossify.

Looking back, that Tuesday merge wasn’t a failure; it was the forge. Jaggedness taught us AI’s no panacea—it’s a tool with teeth, sharp in spots, dull in others. Like Helen Toner put it, models “keep sucking” at the weird stuff, and pretending otherwise bites you. Our lesson? Don’t chase smoothness; map the frontier. Probe the jags with data, hybridize ruthlessly, and remember: In code or cognition, consistency trumps brilliance every time. We’ve got battle scars, sure, but now our AI’s a partner, not a wildcard. And that’s worth every debugged line.

Author’s Note: A Tale from the Trenches

Look, this isn’t some dry whitepaper dissecting LLM token probabilities or benchmarking Grok-4 against o1-preview. It’s a story—ripped from a real (anonymized) postmortem at a dev shop. Why the narrative spin? Because AI jaggedness isn’t an abstract curve on a graph; it’s the gut punch when your “smart” code reviewer greenlights a vuln that tanks production. We dressed it up as fiction to make the jagged edges feel sharp: the 65% hallucination spike on crypto diffs, the RAG pipeline that traded 16 seconds of speed for 70% fewer false positives. If it hooks you into probing your own tools for those hidden cliffs—mission accomplished. Jaggedness won’t smooth out overnight; it’ll keep biting until we stop treating AIs like omniscient oracles and start mapping their quirks like we’d debug a flaky API. Thoughts? Start the discussion below…

entry.title: When Size Isn’t Everything: Why Sapient’s 27M-Parameter HRM Matters for Small Models & AGI
entry.content:
What is HRM (and why we should care)

Singapore’s Sapient Intelligence introduced the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM) — a 27M-parameter, brain-inspired, multi-timescale recurrent architecture trained with just 1,000 examples and no pre-training. According to the authors (arxiv.org), HRM outperforms GPT-o3-mini and Claude on the ARC-AGI benchmark, a test designed to measure genuine inductive reasoning rather than pattern replication.

The design mirrors cognitive neuroscience: the brain separates slow, global planning from fast, fine-grained execution. HRM encodes these separate timescales directly into its architecture.

Empirical Results

Sapient reports:

  • ARC-AGI: HRM surpasses o3-mini-high, Claude 3.7 (8K), and DeepSeek R1 on Sapient’s internal ARC-AGI evaluations (coverage).
  • Structured reasoning tasks: Near-perfect results on Sudoku-Extreme and 30×30 Maze-Hard, where chain-of-thought-dependent LLMs typically break down.
  • Efficiency profile:
    • ~1,000 labeled examples
    • Zero pre-training
    • No chain-of-thought supervision
    • Single-pass inference
    • Over 90% reduction in compute relative to typical LLM reasoning pipelines (ACN Newswire)

The data suggests that architectural inductive bias can outperform sheer parameter scale.

How HRM Works

Hierarchical, Multi-Timescale Architecture

HRM is composed of two interconnected recurrent modules:

  • High-Level Planner
    Slow, abstract reasoning. Responsible for decomposing tasks and constructing coarse strategies.

  • Low-Level Executor
    Fast, detail-oriented operations. Executes logical steps required to satisfy the planner’s subgoals.

This coupled dynamic creates effective depth similar to a deep transformer stack, but with orders of magnitude fewer parameters.

No Chain-of-Thought, No Pre-Training

HRM does not rely on chain-of-thought prompting, large-scale text corpora, or instruction tuning. It performs all reasoning internally and outputs only the final answer.

Benefits include:

  • Lower latency
  • Lower memory footprint
  • Fewer multi-step hallucination/error cascades
  • Simplified deployment on constrained hardware

Data & Compute Efficiency

By learning directly from end-to-end examples, HRM avoids:

  • Billion-token pre-training cycles
  • Long-context inference costs
  • Model distillation or supervised CoT pipelines

Limitations and Open Questions

Although compelling, HRM is not a general-purpose language model:

  • Domain narrowness: Designed for puzzles and abstract reasoning, not open-domain tasks.
  • Reproducibility: Independent results are still sparse.
  • Generalization: Unclear whether this architecture scales to real-world, noisy environments.
  • Opacity: No emitted reasoning trace makes interpretation and debugging harder.

A recent study argues that a 7M-parameter Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) can surpass HRM on ARC-AGI (arxiv.org), hinting that recursion, not hierarchy, may be the core enabler.

Implications: Are Small Models Catching Up?

HRM signals a possible shift in how we think about reasoning systems:

  • Compute accessibility: A 27M-parameter reasoning engine can run on laptops, edge devices, and mid-tier servers.
  • Sparse-data advantages: Scientific reasoning, robotics, and rare-event domains may benefit from models that do not require massive corpora.
  • Hybrid architectures: A small HRM-like module for symbolic reasoning paired with a large LLM for language grounding and world knowledge.

Architectural bias may matter as much as — or more than — raw parameter count.

What to Watch

  • Independent replications of ARC-AGI results
  • Extensions to messy real-world domains
  • LLMs adopting multi-timescale planning modules
  • New interpretability techniques for non-CoT models

HRM doesn’t replace large LLMs, but it questions the assumption that scale alone produces genuine reasoning. The next advances may come from architectural choices rather than parameter inflation.
